title: Internet Message Access Protocol - Version 4rev1
summary: Defines IMAP4rev1, which lets a client access and manipulate email on a server. It allows mailboxes to be handled as if local, supports offline resynchronization, and includes operations to create, delete and rename mailboxes and check for new messages. It was replaced by RFC 9051.

eli5.summary: Instead of downloading your mail and deleting it from the server, IMAP lets you read and organize it where it is stored. It was later replaced by RFC 9051.

questions: what is the difference between imap uid and sequence number
subtitle: How an email client reads and organizes mail that stays on the server, as if the mailboxes were local folders.

tldr.problem: Mail clients need to work with messages stored on a server, including folders, flags and searching, and to resynchronize after being offline, without downloading everything first.
tldr.mechanism: IMAP4rev1 is a line-based text protocol, normally over TCP port 143, in which tagged client commands get untagged data and a tagged OK, NO or BAD result, and a connection moves through four states: not authenticated, authenticated, selected and logout.
tldr.outcome: RFC 3501 was replaced by RFC 9051, and thirteen later RFCs updated it.

today: RFC 3501 was obsoleted by RFC 9051, which is the current version of IMAP, and thirteen later RFCs also updated it. It obsoleted RFC 2060 when it was published as a Proposed Standard.

sections.title: What IMAP4rev1 Does
sections.content:
IMAP4rev1 lets a client access and manipulate email messages on a server. Mailboxes (remote message folders) behave in a way that is functionally equivalent to local folders, and an offline client can resynchronize with the server. The protocol covers creating, deleting and renaming mailboxes, checking for new messages, permanently removing messages, setting and clearing flags, searching, and selectively fetching message attributes, texts and parts of them.

Its limits are stated plainly. It supports a single server; finding configuration for multiple servers is left to RFC 2244. It does not specify how to post mail, which is the job of a mail transfer protocol such as RFC 2821.

The document is written from the point of view of an implementor and says it is not optimized for someone trying to understand the operation of the protocol. Commands (section 6), responses (section 7) and the formal syntax (section 9) must be read together. IMAP4rev1 is designed to be upwards compatible from IMAP2 and unpublished IMAP2bis.
sections.eli5: IMAP is the set of rules that lets your mail app ask the mail server to show, sort, search and delete your messages without carrying them all away.

sections.title: Commands, Responses and Tags
sections.content:
IMAP4rev1 assumes a reliable data stream such as TCP, and a server using TCP listens on port 143. Everything sent is a line ending in CRLF, or a counted run of octets followed by a line.

Each client command starts with a tag, a short string such as A0001 that the client changes for every command. The server sends back untagged data starting with an asterisk and finishes with a tagged completion that repeats the tag: OK for success, NO for failure, or BAD for a protocol error such as an unknown command or a syntax error. A line starting with a plus sign is a continuation request, used when the server is ready for the rest of a command. Servers may also send untagged data on their own, so a client MUST be prepared to accept any server response at any time.

Because of the tags, a client MAY send a new command before the previous one finishes, but not when the commands could affect each other. For example, a FETCH of a message's flags and a STORE of the same message's flags is ambiguous. Since an untagged EXPUNGE can renumber messages, a client that sends any command other than FETCH, STORE or SEARCH MUST wait for its completion before sending a command that uses message sequence numbers. A server's inactivity autologout timer, if it has one, MUST be at least 30 minutes.
sections.eli5: Each question you ask gets a ticket number. The server's answer comes back with the same ticket number and says yes, no, or that you asked it wrongly, so nothing gets mixed up.

sections.title: The Four Connection States
sections.content:
After the connection opens, the server greeting names the starting state. An OK greeting leads to not authenticated, where the client must authenticate before most commands work. A PREAUTH greeting starts the connection already authenticated, and a BYE greeting means the connection was rejected.

A successful LOGIN or AUTHENTICATE moves to the authenticated state, where the client can manage mailboxes but must pick one before touching messages. A successful SELECT or EXAMINE moves to the selected state. A CLOSE, or a failed SELECT or EXAMINE, goes back to authenticated. LOGOUT, server shutdown or a closed connection leads to the logout state.

A command used in the wrong state is a protocol error and gets a BAD or NO. The server MUST NOT unilaterally close the connection without an untagged BYE giving the reason, and a client SHOULD use LOGOUT instead of just closing.
sections.eli5: It is like a building. First you are at the front door, then you are let in, then you open one particular filing cabinet, and finally you leave.

sections.title: Messages, Numbers and Flags
sections.content:
Every message can be reached by one of two numbers. The message sequence number is its relative position, from 1 up to the number of messages, and it can be reassigned during a session: when a message is expunged, the numbers of later messages go down by one. The unique identifier (UID) is a 32-bit value assigned in strictly ascending order that does not change during a session and SHOULD NOT change between sessions.

A mailbox also has a UIDVALIDITY value. Together, the UID and the validity form a 64-bit value that MUST NOT refer to any other message in the mailbox or any later mailbox with the same name forever. If UIDs fail to persist, the validity value MUST be greater than before, which tells an offline client to throw away what it cached.

Flags are named tokens on a message. The system flags are \Seen, \Answered, \Flagged, \Deleted, \Draft and \Recent, and servers may add keywords. Setting \Deleted only marks a message; EXPUNGE or CLOSE removes it for good. Other attributes include the internal date (when the server received it, not the header date), the RFC 2822 size, a parsed envelope and a parsed MIME body structure, and the protocol allows fetching just parts of a message.
sections.eli5: Each letter has a spot in line, which changes when letters leave, and a permanent serial number that never changes. Little stickers like read or important help you sort them.

sections.title: Mailbox Names
sections.content:
Mailbox names are 7-bit. The case-insensitive name INBOX is reserved for the user's primary mailbox on the server; the meaning of every other name depends on the implementation, including whether it is case sensitive. If a server exports hierarchical names, they MUST be left-to-right with one separator character for all levels.

Two conventions are described. A name that begins with a hash sign names a namespace, for example #news.comp.mail.misc for a USENET newsgroup. International names use a modified UTF-7 in which & shifts into a modified BASE64 and a hyphen shifts back, and a literal ampersand is written &-. Because of this, & must not be used as a hierarchy separator.
sections.eli5: Folders get names, and your main inbox always has the same name everywhere. Special codes let folder names use letters from any language.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
IMAP4rev1 sends all traffic, including mail, in the clear unless protection is negotiated, either with STARTTLS, with privacy protection inside AUTHENTICATE, or by some other mechanism. The LOGIN command sends passwords in the clear.

A server MUST be configurable so that at authentication time one of three things holds: STARTTLS has been negotiated, some other mechanism protects against password snooping, or the LOGINDISABLED capability is advertised, plaintext SASL mechanisms are not offered, and LOGIN and plaintext AUTHENTICATE return an error even with a correct password. Implementations MUST support the TLS_RSA_WITH_RC4_128_MD5 cipher suite as a baseline for interoperability.

During TLS negotiation the client MUST check the server hostname it used against the identity in the server certificate, to prevent man-in-the-middle attacks. Error messages for failed logins SHOULD NOT say whether the user name or the password was wrong, and servers SHOULD limit or delay failed attempts.
sections.eli5: Without a lock, anyone listening on the wire can read your mail and password. STARTTLS is the lock, and the server should not tell strangers which part of a guess was wrong.
